raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man presented with acute visual loss in the left eye (LE). The patient denied other ocular or systemic symptoms. He was not taking any medications and his medical, social and family history was unremarkable. Visual acuity (VA) was 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and hand movements in the LE. Slit-lamp examination findings of the anterior segment were normal in both eyes (OU) and intra-ocular pressure was 12 mmHg bilaterally. Dilated fundoscopy of the LE revealed a few vitreous cells and a large yellow macular placoid lesion with a curvilinear edge (Figure 1A (Fig. 1)). Fluorescein angiography (FA) showed early hypofluorescence with late staining in the affected area (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) in the LE demonstrated subretinal fluid overlying the macular lesion (Figure 3 (Fig. 3)). No abnormalities were detected in the RE. Screening blood tests, including syphilis serology, were requested and the patient was monitored without treatment.
Three days after the placoid lesion had extended (Figure 1B (Fig. 1)). The patient did not follow our recommendation for serologic work-up and the tests were ordered again. One week after the initial presentation, VA remained stable but the placoid lesion had increased outside the temporal retinal vascular arcades (Figure 1C (Fig. 1)). New multiple yellow lesions and hemorrhages were observed in the retinal superior nasal area. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) revealed persistent leakage of the choriocapillaris and hypofluorescence areas in the early and late phases (Figure 4 (Fig. 4)). The patient continued not to follow our recommendation for the blood tests and they were ordered for the third time. He was informed again about his clinical situation and the importance of the work-up was underlined. 
The patient abandoned the clinic for two weeks and when observed again, VA had improved to 20/20 in the LE and the lesions showed complete spontaneous resolution (Figure 1D (Fig. 1)). RE examination remained normal. Finally, we had access to the serologic tests results that revealed a positive VDRL (1/128) and FTA-ABS. HIV titers were negative. All other tests were normal. The diagnosis of acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis in the LE was made. The patient was referred to the Infectious Disease Department. He had no other syphilitic manifestations and no abnormalities were detected after computed tomography of the cranium and orbits. A lumbar puncture revealed a positive VDRL and CSF-TPHA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). The patient accepted to start treatment only 45 days after the initial presentation. During this period no relapse of the ocular lesions occurred and no systemic manifestation was observed. The patient was treated with intravenous aqueous penicillin G (four million units given every 4 h for 2 weeks). Three months after treatment, VA was 20/20 and fundoscopy remained normal both eyes. Follow-up serologic testing revealed a decrease of VDRL to 1/32.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old man presented with acute painless visual loss in his left eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with sudden decrease in left eye vision to hand movements without other ocular or systemic complaints. Over the first week of observation (while repeatedly declining ordered blood tests), the left macular placoid lesion expanded beyond the temporal vascular arcades before undergoing complete spontaneous clinical and visual resolution by week 3.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable medical, social, and family history; taking no medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute left visual loss; negative for ocular pain, headache, rash, or other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial ophthalmic examination showed visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye (RE) and hand movements in the left eye (LE), normal bilateral anterior segments, and intraocular pressure of 12 mmHg OU. Left eye dilated fundoscopy revealed mild vitritis (few vitreous cells) and a large yellowish macular placoid lesion with a curvilinear border that expanded over 7 days with superior-nasal yellow lesions and retinal hemorrhages before spontaneously resolving to 20/20 visual acuity and a normal fundus at week 3. Right eye examination was normal throughout.
objective.routine_investigations: Fluorescein angiography (FA) of the left eye showed early hypofluorescence and late macular staining; optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated subretinal fluid overlying the macular lesion; indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed persistent choriocapillaris leakage and early/late hypofluorescence. Blood tests eventually obtained at week 3 revealed reactive serum VDRL (titer 1:128) and positive FTA-ABS, negative HIV serology, and otherwise normal routine labs.
objective.advanced_workup: Cranial and orbital CT was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF analysis revealed reactive CSF VDRL and positive CSF-TPHA confirming neurosyphilis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Unilateral left acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis (ASPPC) with asymptomatic neurosyphilis in an HIV-negative 55-year-old man, confirmed by serum VDRL 1:128, positive serum FTA-ABS, and reactive CSF VDRL and CSF-TPHA. Despite spontaneous resolution of the macular placoid lesion and visual acuity recovery to 20/20 at 3 weeks prior to antibiotic therapy, the patient ultimately consented at day 45 to a 14-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G (4 million units every 4 hours), maintaining 20/20 visual acuity bilaterally and a 4-fold decline in serum VDRL titer (to 1:32) at 3-month follow-up.
